Where a Term's Own Coefficients Begin

Source: R/generics.R
term_coef_start.Rd

Returns the starting coefficients of a built term, one per column of its block. The base method returns zero everywhere, which is an admissible start for a term whose block is a fixed design, since that block does not depend on the coefficients.

Usage

term_coef_start(term, target = NULL, ...)

Arguments

term

A built term (see term_build()). An unbuilt one signals an error through term_npar().

target

Optional numeric vector, one value per observation: the response on the scale of the predictor, NULL by default. It is supplied only where params_interpretation records that the response reads the parameter directly, so a term in a scale's equation receives NULL.

...

Passed to methods. The shipped methods do not use it.

Value

A numeric vector of length term_npar(), in the block's column order.

Why a term supplies a start of its own

A term that recomputes its block from its coefficients (term_refresh()) needs a start of its own, because zero is degenerate for it. In jump() the break-point is read off two coefficients as \(-g_k/\delta_k\), so a vector of zeros puts every break-point at the same clamped position, and with more than one break-point the columns of the block coincide. In seg() the Jacobian column is \(-\gamma_k \mathbb{1}(x > \psi_k)\) and vanishes identically at \(\gamma_k = 0\).

Without a target, the break-point terms return the start that term_build() computed: unit changes, and the break-points at the interior quantiles of the covariate or at the positions that psi names. With a target of the right length and no developed coefficient, the slope and the changes are instead the least-squares coefficients of the target on an intercept and the term's columns at the starting positions. nl() returns the starting values of its own parameters carried through their links.

A coefficient of zero has a meaning that depends on the block that the term builds, so this start belongs to the term, as term_start() does for a structural term.

The role of target

target is the response carried onto the scale of the predictor to which the term contributes. A term cannot compute it, because the term holds its formula and its charts but not the distribution, the link or the equation, which the fitting layer holds. nl() uses it to estimate its own parameters from the data, over a deterministic grid on each free parameter's chart, and the break-point terms use it for the least-squares coefficients described above. Every other term ignores it. The argument is optional; without it each term returns the start that does not depend on the response.

See also

term_start() for a structural term's own parameters, term_refresh() for the terms for which this function exists, seg_start() for the grid rule behind a break-point start.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(50, 0, 10)))

# A fixed design starts at zero.
term_coef_start(term_build(linpar(~ x), dd))
#> [1] 0 0

# A break-point term does not: with several break-points, zero would
# place all of them at the same position.
jb <- term_build(jump(x, npsi = 2), dd)
setNames(term_coef_start(jb), term_coef_names(jb))
#> jump.delta1 jump.delta2     jump.g1     jump.g2 
#>    1.000000    1.000000   -3.847738   -6.908287 

# seg() starts the change at one and the break-point inside the data.
sb <- term_build(seg(x, npsi = 1), dd)
setNames(term_coef_start(sb), term_coef_names(sb))
#>   seg.beta seg.gamma1   seg.psi1 
#>   0.000000   1.000000   5.629448 
range(dd$x)
#> [1] 0.1339033 9.9190609
